questions.q: Which statement correctly describes what superposition means for a qubit in state |+⟩?
options: The qubit is secretly already 0 or already 1, and the 50/50 only reflects our ignorance of which
The qubit genuinely holds both the |0⟩ and |1⟩ amplitudes at once, which is physically different from a hidden pre-existing value
The qubit is randomly switching back and forth between 0 and 1 many times per second
The qubit is in two separate physical locations simultaneously
questions.explain: Superposition means both amplitudes genuinely coexist, not that the qubit secretly has one definite value we simply haven't observed yet. That second picture is a classical probabilistic mixture, and it makes predictions that quantum mechanics violates.

questions.q: What is a 'classical probabilistic mixture' (hidden-variable picture), and why doesn't it correctly describe |+⟩?
options: It's the idea that the qubit has a definite pre-existing value and probability only reflects our ignorance; it fails because it can't explain how H·H deterministically returns |0⟩
It's the idea that qubits don't exist; it fails because qubits have been built in real hardware
It's the idea that measurement always gives 0; it fails because measurement sometimes gives 1
It's the idea that amplitudes must always be positive; it fails because some amplitudes are negative
questions.explain: The hidden-variable picture says the qubit already has a definite value and the 50/50 is just our ignorance. It cannot explain why applying a second Hadamard gate to |+⟩ gives a guaranteed, deterministic |0⟩ every time — a classical mixture has no mechanism for that kind of guaranteed cancellation.

questions.q: H|0⟩ = |+⟩, and H|+⟩ = |0⟩ exactly (H·H = I). Why does this specific fact rule out the hidden-variable picture of |+⟩?
options: It doesn't rule it out — both pictures predict this result equally well

Because a hidden pre-existing value would make the second Hadamard's outcome just another independent random draw, with no mechanism to guarantee a deterministic return to |0⟩ — only interference between amplitudes can do that
Because the Hadamard gate is only defined for |0⟩, not for |+⟩
Because measuring |+⟩ always gives 1, never 0
questions.explain: If |+⟩ really meant a secret, already-decided 0 or 1, a second operation would just add more independent randomness, not guarantee a perfect return to |0⟩. The only way to get that guaranteed outcome is interference between the two amplitudes in |+⟩, which a classical hidden value cannot produce.

questions.q: What is interference, in the sense relevant to superposition, and why can plain classical probabilities never do it?
options: Interference is noise from the environment disturbing the qubit; classical probabilities are also disturbed by noise, so there's no real difference

Interference is amplitudes from different paths adding together before squaring, so they can reinforce or cancel (even to zero); plain probabilities are non-negative numbers that only ever add up, never cancel
Interference is a measurement error that physicists correct for after the fact
Interference only happens when two separate qubits are entangled
questions.explain: Amplitudes are combined before being squared into probabilities, so they can constructively reinforce or destructively cancel. Classical probabilities, being non-negative, can only add — they can never cancel each other out the way amplitudes do.

questions.q: Why does the interference property of superposition matter for quantum computing, beyond being a theoretical curiosity?
options: It doesn't matter for computing — it's purely a philosophical distinction

It means quantum circuits can be designed so wrong answers' amplitudes destructively cancel while the correct answer's amplitude constructively grows, which is the actual source of quantum algorithmic advantage
It matters only because it makes qubits physically smaller than classical bits
It matters only for error correction, not for the core algorithms
questions.explain: Quantum algorithms are engineered sequences of gates that make wrong answers interfere destructively and the correct answer interfere constructively. If superposition were just classical ignorance, there would be no amplitudes to interfere, and this entire algorithmic strategy would be impossible.
